guide.title: Throgs Neck, the Bronx: Fort Schuyler at the Peninsula's Tip
guide.intro: Throgs Neck is a peninsula in the southeastern Bronx, 1.903 square miles (4.93 km²) bounded by the East River and Long Island Sound to the south and east, Westchester Creek on the west, and Baisley Avenue and the Bruckner Expressway on the north. At its tip, where the East River meets the Sound, stands Fort Schuyler, a Third System coastal fortification built between 1833 and 1856 and the campus of SUNY Maritime College since 1938. The Throgs Neck Bridge carries Interstate 295 from the peninsula across to Bay Terrace in Queens. Also on the peninsula are Silver Beach and the Locust Point enclave, Preston High School in the Havemeyer-Huntington mansion, Monsignor Scanlan High School and St. Joseph's School for the Deaf on the Hutchinson River Parkway, and a public library branch on the Cross Bronx Expressway. The ZIP code is 10465; the 2011 population was 21,009.

sections.heading: Out on the peninsula
sections.body:
Fort Schuyler holds the southeastern tip, where the East River meets Long Island Sound, and SUNY Maritime College's address there is 6 Pennyfield Avenue. Inside the fort are the Stephen B. Luce Library, administrative offices, the Marine Transportation Department and the Maritime Industry Museum, established in 1986. The Havemeyer-Huntington mansion, at 2780 Schurz Avenue, is Preston High School. Monsignor Scanlan High School is at 915 Hutchinson River Parkway and St. Joseph's School for the Deaf at 1000 Hutchinson River Parkway — two addresses on one road, and two halves of what was a single campus until the parkway extension cut it in two in 1939. The New York Public Library's Throg's Neck branch is at 3025 Cross Bronx Expressway; a Sesame Street mural covers the north wall of its courtyard, and the branch is fully accessible, with collections for adults, young adults and children.

The Throgs Neck Bridge crosses from the peninsula to Bay Terrace in Queens, carrying Interstate 295. Othmar Ammann designed it, as he designed the George Washington, Bronx–Whitestone, Verrazzano-Narrows and Triborough bridges. Ground was broken on October 22, 1957 and the bridge opened on January 11, 1961, at a construction cost of $92,000,000. It is a suspension bridge of six lanes, 11,250 feet (3,430 m) long including approaches, with a center span of 1,800 feet (550 m), towers 346 feet (105 m) tall and 142 feet (43 m) of clearance below; each main cable is made of 37 strands of 296 wires, 10,952 wires to a cable. It was built to relieve the Bronx–Whitestone Bridge, two miles west. Twenty thousand vehicles crossed in its first twelve hours, 16.4 million in 1961, its first full year, and daily traffic in 2016 was 119,249. Peregrine falcons have nested on the bridge since at least 1983. Tolls as of January 4, 2026 were $12.03 by mail, $7.46 with a New York E-ZPass and $9.79 at the mid-tier E-ZPass rate.

Locust Point is a related area within Throggs Neck, bounded by Harding Avenue to the north, the Throgs Neck Bridge to the east, and Eastchester Bay: 0.416 square miles, with a population of 1,479 and a median income of $85,072 as of 2011. It was originally Wrights Island, after its owner Captain J. T. Wright, and then Locust Island, until the waterway separating it was filled — the same landfill that carries the Throgs Neck Bridge's northern ramp and toll plaza — turning the former island into a peninsula. The Locust Point Yacht Club occupies the outermost block before the bay, at 21 Longstreet Avenue. Michael Kay is a former resident.

Community District 10 is patrolled by the 45th Precinct of the NYPD, at 2877 Barkley Avenue in Throggs Neck. Two FDNY stations stand in Throggs Neck: Engine Company 89 and Ladder Company 50 at 2924 Bruckner Boulevard, and Engine Company 72 with Satellite 2 at 3929 East Tremont Avenue.

sections.heading: Vriedelandt, Throckmorton and the Battle of Throgs Neck
sections.body:
The New Netherlanders called the peninsula Vriedelandt, "Land of Peace." The current name comes from John Throckmorton, an English immigrant and an associate of Roger Williams, whom the Dutch allowed to settle the area in 1642 with thirty-five others; at the same time the peninsula was also known as Maxson's point. Many of the settlers, Anne Hutchinson among them, were killed in a 1643 uprising, and Throckmorton returned to Rhode Island. By 1668 the peninsula appeared on maps as Frockes Neck, and it was virtually an island at high tide.

In 1776 George Washington's headquarters wrote of a potential British landing at Frogs Neck. It came that October. At the bridge over Westchester Creek, now represented by an unobtrusive steel and concrete span at East Tremont Avenue near Westchester Avenue, General Howe made an unsuccessful effort to cut off Washington's troops; when the British approached, the Americans ripped up the plank bridge and opened a heavy fire that forced Howe to withdraw and change his plans. Six days later Howe landed troops at Rodman's Neck to the north, on the far side of Eastchester Bay.

A farm owned by the Stephenson family was sold in 1795 to Abijah Hammond, who built a mansion that later became the offices of the Silver Beach Garden Corporation. The Morris family purchased land around 1848 and built two mansions on it. The estate that had belonged to Havemeyer and then to Collis P. Huntington carried the Havemeyer-Huntington mansion, which is now home to Preston High School. Silver Beach Garden was formed by the Peters and Sorgenfrel families.

People born or raised in Throggs Neck include Christine Jorgensen, the first transgender celebrity of the 1950s and 1960s, following her surgical transformation in Denmark in 1952, who was born and raised on Dudley Avenue; Doug Marrone, head coach of the Jacksonville Jaguars; Bill Polian, a Hall of Fame executive in the National Football League; and Frank Bello, Charlie Benante, Michael Kay, Sal Mineo, T.J. Rivera and Ritchie Torres.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No subway line reaches Throgs Neck. A plan drawn between 1929 and 1939 for a Second Avenue Subway branch to Throggs Neck never materialized. The nearest subway is Westchester Square–East Tremont Avenue, at the intersection of East Tremont and Westchester Avenues, in Westchester Square and on the border of the Pelham Bay neighborhoods; its northbound platform gives a view of the Bronx–Whitestone and Throgs Neck Bridges. Buhre Avenue station, at the intersection of Buhre and Westchester Avenues, is in Pelham Bay.

Buses serve the neighborhood instead. The routes include the Bx8, the Bx40 and Bx42, the Q44 SBS, the Q50 and BxM9 express service. The Bx8 runs between Locust Point, at Longstreet Avenue and Tierney Place, and Williamsbridge, at East 226th Street and White Plains Road, by way of Throgs Neck Boulevard, Crosby Avenue, Williamsbridge Road and Bronxwood Avenue, connecting at its northern end to the 225th Street station on the IRT White Plains Road Line, served by the 2 and 5; some rush hour trips terminate or originate at Westchester Square. The Bx40 and Bx42 connect Morris Heights, at River Park Towers, with SUNY Maritime College and Throgs Neck at Harding Avenue and Emerson Avenue.

No Metro-North station serves Throgs Neck. Penn Station Access's Phase One is adding four Metro-North stations in the Bronx — Co-op City, Morris Park, Parkchester/Van Nest and Hunts Point — and Throgs Neck is not among them.

NYC Ferry's Throggs Neck stop opened on December 28, 2021, when the Soundview route was extended there. The Soundview route itself launched on August 15, 2018, serving East 34th Street in Manhattan, and a Stuyvesant Cove stop was added in May 2020. In July 2025 the New York City Economic Development Corporation announced a plan to merge the Rockaway and Soundview routes, finalized in November 2025.

By road, the Throgs Neck Bridge carries Interstate 295 between the peninsula and Bay Terrace in Queens.

faq.question: How do I get to Throgs Neck?
faq.answer: Not by subway: no line reaches the peninsula. The nearest station is Westchester Square–East Tremont Avenue, at the intersection of East Tremont and Westchester Avenues, in Westchester Square and on the border of the Pelham Bay neighborhoods, with Buhre Avenue, at Buhre and Westchester Avenues, in Pelham Bay. Buses serving the neighborhood include the Bx8, the Bx40 and Bx42, the Q44 SBS, the Q50 and BxM9 express service; the Bx40 and Bx42 run from Morris Heights to SUNY Maritime College and to Harding Avenue and Emerson Avenue, and the Bx8 has its southern terminal at Longstreet Avenue and Tierney Place in Locust Point. NYC Ferry's Throggs Neck stop, on the Soundview route, opened on December 28, 2021. No Metro-North station serves the neighborhood. By road, the Throgs Neck Bridge carries Interstate 295 from Bay Terrace in Queens.

faq.question: Why is it called Throgs Neck?
faq.answer: For John Throckmorton, an English immigrant and an associate of Roger Williams, whom the Dutch allowed to settle the peninsula in 1642 with thirty-five others. faq.question: What is Fort Schuyler?
faq.answer: A coastal fortification at the southeastern tip of Throggs Neck, where the East River meets Long Island Sound, built between 1833 and 1856 as an example of the Third System of American coastal fortifications. At its peak it held 312 guns and could accommodate 1,250 personnel. It was designated a New York City individual landmark on April 19, 1966 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 29, 1976. It has been the campus of SUNY Maritime College since 1938, and houses the college's Stephen B. Luce Library, administrative offices, Marine Transportation Department and the Maritime Industry Museum, established in 1986.

When the British approached, the Americans ripped up the plank bridge and opened a heavy fire that forced Howe to withdraw and change his plans. Six days later Howe landed troops at Rodman's Neck to the north, on the far side of Eastchester Bay.

faq.question: What is the Throgs Neck Bridge?
faq.answer: A suspension bridge carrying Interstate 295 between Throggs Neck and Bay Terrace in Queens, designed by Othmar Ammann, who also designed the George Washington, Bronx–Whitestone, Verrazzano-Narrows and Triborough bridges. Ground was broken on October 22, 1957 and it opened on January 11, 1961 at a cost of $92,000,000. It runs 11,250 feet (3,430 m) including approaches, with a center span of 1,800 feet (550 m) and 142 feet (43 m) of clearance below, and it was built to relieve the Bronx–Whitestone Bridge, two miles west. Peregrine falcons have nested on it since at least 1983.

photos.title: The Throgs Neck peninsula from the air
photos.description: An aerial view down the length of the Throgs Neck peninsula, photographed through an aircraft window. The Throgs Neck Bridge crosses the water in the lower half of the frame, the star-shaped walls of Fort Schuyler sit on the point beyond it alongside the playing fields and buildings of the SUNY Maritime College campus, and marinas, small-boat basins and low-rise housing fill the shore.
photos.author: D. Benjamin Miller

places.name: Fort Schuyler and SUNY Maritime College
places.summary: A coastal fortification at the southeastern tip of Throggs Neck, where the East River meets Long Island Sound, built between 1833 and 1856 and now the campus of SUNY Maritime College. The fort houses the Stephen B. Luce Library, administrative offices, the Marine Transportation Department and the Maritime Industry Museum, established in 1986. It was designated a New York City individual landmark on April 19, 1966 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 29, 1976, reference number 76001206, at the address "Throggs Neck at East River and Long Island Sound".
places.history:
The fort was built between 1833 and 1856, exemplifying the Third System of United States coastal fortifications. At its peak it housed 312 guns and could accommodate 1,250 personnel: the bottom two tiers inside the fort were casemated, while the third tier on the roof had barbette mounts, and the works included two demi-bastions, a ravelin, flank howitzers, an extensive hornwork — unique in the third system — and an advanced redoubt, later demolished. It was dedicated in 1856 but not garrisoned until 1861. During the Civil War it held up to 500 Confederate prisoners and contained the McDougall Hospital, with a 2,000-bed capacity. Endicott-era coastal artillery from 3-inch to 12-inch caliber was installed between 1898 and 1900, and some armaments were removed between 1917 and 1920. The fort was transferred to New York State in 1934 and its restoration was completed by the Works Progress Administration.

SUNY Maritime College was established in 1874 as the New York Nautical School, the oldest institution of its kind in the United States. It moved to the Fort Schuyler campus in 1938, became degree-granting in 1946, joined the SUNY system in 1948 and took its current name in 1949. The campus covers 55 acres. Fall 2025 enrollment was 1,552 students, 1,402 undergraduate and 150 postgraduate. Its bachelor's degrees prepare graduates for licensure as third mate or third assistant engineer in the U.S. Merchant Marine; it offers master's degrees in International Transportation Management and in Maritime and Naval Studies, and runs the only Navy and Marine Corps ROTC program in the New York metropolitan area. Its teams, the Privateers, compete in NCAA Division III in the Skyline Conference across 16 varsity sports. Alumni include Scott Kelly, Gary Jobson, Harry Manning and Joseph Hazelwood, captain of the Exxon Valdez.

photos.title: Fort Schuyler: the middle bastion
photos.description: The granite outer wall of Fort Schuyler, showing the angled middle bastion and two tiers of small openings cut through the masonry, with mown lawn in the foreground and bare trees at the right.
photos.author: Trevor Webb

photos.title: SUNY Maritime College from the water
photos.description: The SUNY Maritime College waterfront seen from the water on an overcast day: a pale tower rising above lower campus buildings, the grey stonework of Fort Schuyler and its railing at the left, and a kayaker paddling past the seawall in the foreground.
photos.author: Julie McCoy (Kayak Cowgirl)

places.name: Preston High School
places.summary: A private, all-female high school at 2780 Schurz Avenue, occupying the Havemeyer-Huntington mansion. It was founded in 1947 by the Sisters of the Divine Compassion and named for Monsignor Thomas Scott Preston, who with Mother Mary Veronica founded the order. Its motto is Virtus Mille Scuta.
places.history: Havemeyer purchased the property in 1863 from the heirs of Dominick Lynch Lawrence, and Huntington acquired it in 1884. The Sisters of the Divine Compassion bought the estate in 1927 and ran it as the House of the Holy Family before converting it to a high school in 1947. The campus was expanded in 1960 and again in 1965. The school's logo was modified in 1997 to incorporate the Throgs Neck Bridge, representing a bridge to opportunity. In 2025 the school reached a 25-year, $8.5 million deal with the Ballys Foundation.

photos.title: Preston High School entrance
photos.description: The front entrance of Preston High School: a light brick facade with a band of windows above a recessed porch, red-framed glass doors, and the school's monogram and lettering carved into the panel over the doorway, approached by a paved walk with flowers on either side.
photos.author: Sadia Romain

places.name: Monsignor Scanlan High School
places.summary: A Roman Catholic coeducational high school at 915 Hutchinson River Parkway, in the Archdiocese of New York and affiliated with the Dominican Sisters of Sparkill. Its campus covers 13 acres, and it is accredited by the Middle States Association and the Board of Regents.
places.history: St. Helena's Elementary School opened in 1940. In 1949 the parish purchased land from St. Joseph's School for the Deaf in Throggs Neck and established two high schools that year, St. Helena's High School for Boys and St. Helena's High School for Girls. Both were renamed in Monsignor Arthur J. Scanlan's honor in 1972, merged into a single coeducational institution in 1976, and became administratively independent from the parish in 2014. Approximately 460 students were enrolled as of 2021. The school offers Advanced Placement courses and STEM programs, and its athletic programs include baseball, basketball, softball, volleyball, track and cross country.

places.name: St. Joseph's School for the Deaf
places.summary: A Catholic school for deaf students in Throggs Neck, on a 10-acre campus at 1000 Hutchinson River Parkway, serving grades from infancy through the eighth grade across a main school, a daycare and a pre-school. Its own site gives the tagline "A School for All Seasons, Since 1869".
places.history: The school was founded in 1869 by Victorine Boucher and the Society of the Daughters of the Heart of Mary as Saint Joseph's Institute for the Improved Instruction of Deaf Mutes, at 772 East 188th Street in Fordham. It established its present Throggs Neck site in 1876 on land bought from Charles Lochran, and a branch in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, operated from 1874 to 1936. A second building went up in 1897 to a design by Schickel & Ditmars, and the current brick Romanesque Revival building, by the same architects, was completed in 1913. The extension of the Hutchinson River Parkway divided the campus in two in 1939, and in 1949 the western portion was transferred to become Monsignor Scanlan High School. The residential program ended in 1950.

places.name: New York Public Library, Throg's Neck Branch
places.summary: A New York Public Library branch at 3025 Cross Bronx Expressway. It is fully accessible and holds collections for adults, young adults and children, and a Sesame Street mural covers the north wall of its courtyard.
places.history: The branch has operated since 1954 and moved to its current one-story building in 1974, which opened that September.

places.name: Locust Point Yacht Club
places.summary: A yacht club at 21 Longstreet Avenue, in Locust Point, occupying the outermost block before the bay.
places.history: Locust Point is bounded by Harding Avenue to the north, the Throgs Neck Bridge to the east, and Eastchester Bay. It was originally Wrights Island, after its owner Captain J. T. Wright, and then Locust Island, until the waterway separating it was filled — the same landfill that carries the Throgs Neck Bridge's northern ramp and toll plaza — turning the former island into a peninsula.

links.note: City Island and Throgs Neck are both part of Bronx Community District 10, along with Country Club, Pelham Bay, Schuylerville and Westchester Square.
